message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
Here's everything. The route is first, because there's only one order that works and it leaves no spare time.

## Route and timeline: B → A → C

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive **B** (20 min drive) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B, done before the 09:30 opening ✓ |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive to **A** (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A, inside the 09:00–10:00 window ✓ |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive to **C** (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break** while waiting for C to open |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at C, no earlier than 11:00 ✓ |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive back to depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | Back at depot ✓ |

**Why this is the only order:**
- **A before B fails.** The van reaches A at 09:00 at the earliest, finishes at 09:15, then gets to B at 09:40, after the 09:30 opening.
- **C can't come before A or B.** C won't accept anything before 11:00, and by then both other windows have closed.

**The catch: there's no slack at all.** The van gets back at exactly 12:00. Any delay at C means it's late: a slow handover, a hunt for parking, a queue at reception. To build in some margin:
- Call C and ask whether they'd take delivery at 10:45. That gives 15 minutes in hand, though the break would then have to come before 10:45.
- Ask whether "back by 12:00" can stretch to 12:15 if needed.
- At minimum, phone C ahead so someone is ready to receive at 11:00 sharp.

## Van name ideas
- **Chester**, as in chest of drawers
- **Dovetail**
- **Patina**
- **Sideboard Sid**
- **The Chaise**

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Company] is on its way! [Driver] should be with you around [time]. Please make sure someone's in to receive it. Thanks!

## Three checks before handover
1. **Condition.** Look for scratches, chips or marks in the finish picked up in transit. Compare against the photos taken before loading.
2. **Function and stability.** Check that drawers and doors open smoothly, legs are firm, and joints and hardware are secure.
3. **Completeness.** Make sure it's the right piece, with every part: shelves, glass, keys, fixings, and any extras that come with the order.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Email**, with the customer's signature and a photo captured on a phone or tablet at the door. It's harder to lose and easy to find if there's ever a dispute. Keep paper copies in the van for customers who'd rather have one.

## Proof of delivery, in a line

"A record, usually a signature, photo and time, showing the item was handed over to the right person, at the right address, in good condition."

## Evening-before text

> Hi [Name], it's [Company]. Your delivery is booked for tomorrow, roughly [9:30-10:30am]. Reply here if that's a problem. Thanks!

With a typical name and company filled in, that's about 135 characters, so it stays under 160. Two things that can push a text over the limit:
- **Long names.** Check the longest company name you'll use.
- **Emoji and curly apostrophes (' instead of ').** Either can switch the message to an encoding with a 70-character limit, which would split it into several texts. Keep apostrophes straight and leave out emoji.
